Wonder, labor, identity · 2001

Spirited AwayThe Work of Becoming Yourself

Marina considers Spirited Away’s bathhouse, sound, moral ambiguity, and vivid imagination, while noting where its episodic storytelling feels overfull.

By MarinaOctober 17, 20263 min readSpoiler-light review

In this review

A World Built from Work and WonderThe Tenderness of UncertaintySources & references
Film
Spirited Away
Director
Hayao Miyazaki
Year
2001

Hayao Miyazaki’s Spirited Away begins with a child who does not want to move, then lets the world around her become stranger than her reluctance. Chihiro enters a spirit world organized by appetite, labor, names, and rules she cannot yet read. The premise is simple enough to follow, but the film’s feeling is not: wonder arrives beside unease, and beauty often has something hungry beneath it. I find its imagination most persuasive when it treats the fantastic as an extension of ordinary social pressure.

A World Built from Work and Wonder

The bathhouse is the film’s great visual invention, a vertical, crowded workplace where gods arrive to be cleaned and exhausted workers keep the machinery moving. Miyazaki fills every corner with motion: pipes tremble, doors slide, creatures queue, steam obscures the distance. This abundance never feels like decoration alone. The setting makes Chihiro’s growth practical; she learns by observing gestures, timing, and the dignity of doing an unglamorous task properly. Animation here is not escape from the material world but a way of making its demands visible.

Sound gives the film an equally careful architecture. Joe Hisaishi’s score can open into luminous travel, then retreat until footsteps, water, or a room’s low hum become expressive. Silence is not emptiness; it gives Chihiro space to register what she cannot explain. The voice performances, especially Rumi Hiiragi’s changing energy as Chihiro, keep the character grounded amid impossible company. Her fear is audible, but so is her concentration. She becomes brave less through speeches than through the steady accumulation of small decisions.

What I admire most is the film’s refusal to divide its spirits neatly into good and evil. Some figures are frightening because they are lonely, vain, or overburdened; others become kind without becoming harmless. That moral looseness gives the encounters a human scale, and it keeps the story from turning into a lesson with one approved answer. At the same time, the episodic middle can feel overfull. Its parade of inventions sometimes delays emotional transitions, as if the film trusts its world more readily than its connective tissue.

The Tenderness of Uncertainty

The film also has a sharp eye for the costs of consumption. Food, gold, cleanliness, and work circulate through the bathhouse as pleasures and obligations, while the natural world appears wounded by what people discard. These ideas are present without being pinned to a single speech, which I appreciate. Miyazaki lets images carry the argument: a body becomes a problem to be handled, a river carries a memory, a train crosses a quiet expanse. The symbols are clear, but the mood around them remains beautifully unsettled.

Spirited Away stays with me because it understands that growing up is not a clean departure from strangeness. It is learning how to move through systems that are absurd, beautiful, and occasionally cruel without surrendering one’s attention to others. The film’s richest moments are pauses between spectacles, when a character waits, listens, or shares a modest kindness. Its few crowded passages may test patience, but they also belong to its generosity. This is fantasy with room for uncertainty, and that room is where its tenderness lives.
